title: Acylation of pyrrole
subtitle: Pyrrole attacks acetic anhydride at C-2, with no Lewis acid

reactants.caption: pyrrole + acetic anhydride
reactants.learnerPrompt: Pyrrole attacks acetic anhydride. Draw the attack from the carbon next to nitrogen, and let the nitrogen lone pair take the positive charge.
hintTiers: Pyrrole is an electron-rich ring, like an enamine: its nitrogen lone pair is part of the aromatic sextet. Which ring carbon is the nucleophile, and what is the electrophile in acetic anhydride?

A ring π bond attacks a carbonyl carbon of the anhydride, and that C=O π bond moves onto oxygen. The positive charge left on the ring is best drawn on nitrogen: the other ring π bond shifts along and the nitrogen lone pair forms a C=N π bond. Up to four arrows.

The π bond from the carbon next to nitrogen (the one with the drawn H) → a new bond to a carbonyl carbon; that C=O π bond → a lone pair on its oxygen; the far ring π bond → the middle ring bond; the nitrogen lone pair → a π bond to the far carbon next to it.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: The nitrogen lone pair is part of the aromatic sextet. Using it to make a new bond would destroy the aromaticity, so pyrrole is neither basic nor nucleophilic at nitrogen. It reacts at carbon.

Attack at C-3 does happen, but it is slower. The cation it gives can share its charge between only one carbon and nitrogen; attack next to nitrogen gives a cation spread over two carbons and nitrogen. Attack from the carbon next to nitrogen.

Attack at C-3 (or C-4) does happen, but it is slower. The cation it gives can share its charge between only one carbon and nitrogen; attack next to nitrogen gives a cation spread over two carbons and nitrogen. Attack from the carbon next to nitrogen.
The oxygens of the anhydride are electron-rich. The electrophile is a carbonyl carbon.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right ring carbon and right electrophile, but the carbonyl carbon now has five bonds. Move its C=O π bond onto oxygen.

tetrahedral-intermediate.caption: the tetrahedral intermediate: an iminium ion and an alkoxide
tetrahedral-intermediate.learnerPrompt: The tetrahedral intermediate collapses. Draw it.
hintTiers: The alkoxide oxygen can push back down to re-form a C=O bond. Which group on that carbon leaves?
Re-forming C=O pushes out a leaving group: acetate is a much better leaving group than the ring carbon. Two arrows.
The O⁻ lone pair → the C=O π bond; the bond from that carbon to the ester oxygen → a lone pair on that oxygen (acetate leaves).

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Breaking the bond to the ring just goes back to the start. Acetate is the better leaving group: let it go.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Acetate does leave, but the carbon would be left with three bonds. Bring the O⁻ lone pair down to make C=O.

acylpyrrolium.caption: the protonated 2-acetylpyrrole (an iminium ion) + acetate
acylpyrrolium.learnerPrompt: Acetate removes a proton and the ring becomes aromatic again.
hintTiers: The ring has one sp³ carbon. Which hydrogen goes, and where do its electrons go?
Acetate takes the H on the sp³ carbon. The C–H electrons make a ring π bond, the ring π bonds shift along, and the C=N π bond returns to nitrogen as its lone pair. Four arrows.
Acetate O⁻ lone pair → a new O–H bond to the ring H; that C–H bond → the π bond to the next ring carbon; the ring C=C π bond → the next ring bond; the C=N π bond → a lone pair on nitrogen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Adding acetate back to the ketone just reverses the last step. Acetate acts as a base here: the ring wants its aromaticity back.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right proton. Now the C–H bonding electrons must go into the ring, and the C=N π bond back onto nitrogen.

steps.explanationAfterStep: Pyrrole is so electron-rich that it needs no Lewis acid: the anhydride itself is electrophilic enough. Attack next to nitrogen gives a cation spread over three atoms, and the best drawing puts the charge on nitrogen, with every atom an octet (an iminium ion). Stopping with the charge on a ring carbon is also accepted: it is another drawing of the same cation.
As in any substitution at a carbonyl group, the tetrahedral intermediate collapses and the better leaving group, acetate, goes.
Losing the proton restores the aromatic ring. The product is a ketone conjugated with the ring, so it is far less nucleophilic than pyrrole and does not react a second time.

mechanismSummary: Pyrrole is an enamine built into an aromatic ring, so it is far more nucleophilic than benzene and reacts with acetic anhydride without a Lewis acid. Attack comes from C-2, next to nitrogen, because the cation formed there is spread over three atoms, one of them nitrogen (attack at C-3 gives only two). The tetrahedral intermediate loses acetate, and acetate removes the proton from the sp³ ring carbon to restore aromaticity: 2-acetylpyrrole.
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 29
